title: The staircase
hookLine: a man building a staircase to a palace he has never seen

lines: A MAN AT A CROSSROADS, BUILDING.
cards: A debating hall in Savatthi, full of wandering ascetics, and loud. They're talking about kings, robbers, armies, food, gossip. Their leader, Potthapada, sees the Buddha coming in the distance and hushes them.
Quiet, friends. Here comes the recluse Gotama. He likes quiet.

The ninth long discourse is the long conversation that follows, about perception, the self, and how anyone could know. And in the middle of it, the Buddha describes a man at a crossroads, building a staircase.

teach.b: Some teachers of the time said that after death the self is perfectly happy. The Buddha asks them simple questions. Do you know a world that's perfectly happy?

teach.h: HAVE YOU SEEN EVEN ONE HAPPY DAY?
teach.b: Have you ever experienced even a single day, or a single night, of perfect happiness? No. Do you know a path that leads there?

teach.h: A STAIRCASE TO AN UNSEEN PALACE
teach.b: A man is building a staircase at a crossroads, to climb up into a palace. Someone asks: this palace, do you know where it is? East, west, north, south?
Tall or short? No, I don't know. So you're building a staircase to a palace you don't know and have never seen?
Yes. The Pali for staircase is nissenni, and the palace is pasada. Isn't that talk, the Buddha asks, without any foundation?
The point isn't that hope is foolish. It's about honesty. If you claim certainty about a destination, it's fair to ask whether anyone has seen it, including you.
Then a quieter teaching. Near the end, a man named Citta presses on the self, and the Buddha says the ways we name a self are like milk, curd and butter.

When it's milk, nobody calls it curd; when it's curd, nobody calls it butter. These are the world's ordinary names, and the Buddha uses them, without being taken in by them. So the staircase cuts two ways.
Don't build toward something no one has seen. And don't mistake the names on each step for something fixed.
Build where you can see where you're going, in experience you can test, one step at a time.

how: Buddhist teachers encourage students to test teachings in their own experience rather than accept claims about unseen states, and they speak of 'conventional' language as useful without being taken as ultimate.

o: the stages of meditation, climbed in order
steps built toward a palace never seen
a ladder up to the highest heaven

p: the wanderer who hushed the hall

s: the teachers in DN 9 had experienced the perfect happiness they promised
asked if they'd known even one perfectly happy day or night, they say no.
Potthapada hushed his friends because the Buddha likes quiet
the hall was loud with talk of kings, robbers and gossip.
the Buddha refuses to use ordinary words like 'self'
he uses the world's names, like milk, curd and butter, without being taken in by them.

games.q: you meet a man building a staircase at a crossroads to climb into a palace. you ask where the palace is. what does he say?
games.why: he doesn't know which direction, or how tall. the Buddha uses him for any claim about a destination no one has seen.

practice: Pick one thing you're working toward, a promotion, a move, a version of yourself, and picture the staircase you're building.
Ask the man's questions: where exactly is the palace, have I tasted even a day of it, what do I actually know? You don't have to stop building; just see what's real under the steps.

wordCard.voice: The staircase. A man building steps toward a palace he's never seen: claims without foundation, and names mistaken for things.

orig.note: Pali nissenni: staircase, ladder. built toward a pasada, a palace, that no one has seen.

carryVoice: Your line: a staircase to where. Milk, curd, butter: names to use without being taken in. Day five hundred thirty-six, done.
